The Collared aracari (Pteroglossus torquatus) is a medium-sized toucan inhabiting lowland forests from southern Mexico to Colombia. Neonates emerge from the egg at a remarkably modest size, with initial body mass averaging 10 grams [Wwb = 10 grams], a value consistent with the altricial developmental mode typical of ramphastids. Field studies indicate that incubation at a steady temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] yields a hatching period of between 15 and 18 days, with a central tendency of approximately 16.5 days [ab = approximately 16.5 days], reflecting the thermal sensitivity of embryonic development in this lineage. The altricial hatchlings are brooded intensively by both parents, relying on parental provisioning during the initial weeks of life, during which they gain mass steadily through a diet rich in fruit pulp and arthropod prey delivered by adults.

Under the typical active metabolic conditions that prevail during the breeding season in this species, characterized by a body temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C], the nestling period progresses through a predictable sequence of developmental milestones. Fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight and departure from the nest cavity, occurs at approximately 42 days after hatching [tx = approximately 42 days after hatching], a duration that is relatively protracted compared to smaller passerines but typical for toucans, which exhibit slow growth rates linked to their frugivorous diet and the energetic demands of cavity nesting at a temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. The fledglings remain dependent on parental care for several additional weeks, gradually transitioning to independent foraging as their flight proficiency improves. This developmental schedule places considerable energetic pressure on the breeding adults, which must maintain high provisioning rates throughout this extended nestling period to ensure successful recruitment of offspring into the population.

The species exhibits a distinctly slow life-history pace, with the onset of reproductive maturity deferred well beyond the completion of somatic growth. Puberty, defined by the initiation of gonadal activity and the onset of spermatogenesis and follicular development, is reached at approximately 126 days after hatching [tp = approximately 126 days after hatching] when individuals are maintained at 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. This relatively late maturation, while accelerated relative to larger toucan species, still represents a substantial delay compared to many frugivorous birds of equivalent body size. The deferral is likely adaptive, allowing young birds to acquire the foraging skills and social dominance necessary to secure nesting territories and attract mates. First-year birds frequently remain as non-breeding floaters within the population, only entering the breeding pool once suitable cavities and mates become available, which further extends the interval between hatching and first successful reproduction.

The age at first successful reproduction, encompassing the full cycle from pair formation through egg-laying and hatching of the first brood, is substantially later than the onset of mere physiological maturity. Under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic metabolism (41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]), first reproduction is recorded at approximately 1095 days after hatching [tR = approximately 1095 days after hatching], indicating that young birds delay breeding for nearly three years after hatching even though they are physiologically capable of reproduction much earlier. This prolonged interval likely reflects the challenges of cavity acquisition in a competitive environment, the time required to develop effective foraging proficiency, and the need to accumulate sufficient body reserves to support the energetic demands of egg production and parental care. Comparative data from other ramphastids suggest this life-history pattern is broadly shared across the family, with larger species tending to exhibit even more pronounced delays in first reproduction.

The ultimate adult body mass attained by Collared aracari averages 155 grams [Wwi = 155 grams], a figure that falls below the 230 grams reported by some historical compilations but is consistent with more recent field measurements from Central American populations. Both parents share in the reproductive effort, and the species exhibits a single annual clutch of three eggs [N_R_i = clutch of three eggs], with one clutch produced each year [F_R_i = one clutch produced each year]. This low annual reproductive output, combined with a maximum lifespan estimated at approximately 6022 days [am = approximately 6022 days] when assessed at 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C], underscores the species' placement on the slow end of the life-history continuum among Neotropical frugivorous birds. The extended lifespan, comparable to that of the larger toco toucan (Ramphastos toco), likely reflects the reduced predation pressure associated with cavity nesting and the relatively low metabolic costs of a frugivorous diet in a stable tropical environment.
